analysis.one_liner: Bars forced arbitration and class-action waivers in employee retirement and health benefit plans.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced with zero cosponsors in the final weeks of the session, it was sent to the Senate labor committee and died there when Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the federal law governing employer-sponsored retirement and health benefit plans (ERISA) to make forced arbitration clauses, class-action waivers, and "discretionary" clauses unenforceable in plan documents. Workers and retirees could then take disputes over their benefits or their retirement savings to court, including as class actions. It would also bar plans from requiring workers to give up those rights as a condition of participating in a plan or receiving benefits.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and retirees covered by employer-sponsored retirement and health plans — especially the tens of millions enrolled in 401(k)-style plans whose documents route disputes over fees, mismanagement, or denied benefits into individual arbitration. If the bill passed, they could sue in court, join class actions to recover small individual losses, and get an independent judge to re-review a denied benefit from scratch instead of a standard that defers to the plan administrator.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and retirees in employer benefit plans

how_it_helps.text: Makes mandatory pre-dispute arbitration clauses unenforceable in ERISA plan disputes, so a worker or retiree cannot be forced out of court before a dispute ever happens.

Allows post-dispute arbitration only under strict conditions: no coercion or threat of losing benefits, a plain-language written notice of the right to refuse, a 45-day waiting period, and affirmative written consent — protecting workers who are pressured to sign away their rights to keep a job or benefits.
Bans class-action and collective-claim waivers, letting workers pool small-dollar claims (such as excessive 401(k) fees) that are uneconomical to bring one at a time.
Invalidates 'discretionary' clauses and requires courts to review denied benefit claims from scratch (de novo), rather than deferring to the plan administrator's own interpretation of the plan.

Prohibits plans, employers, and plan administrators from including these clauses in plan documents at all, and lets the Labor Department write regulations to enforce the rules; the restrictions apply to claims arising after enactment even if plan documents haven't been updated yet.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that sponsor plans, plan administrators, and benefits service providers, who would face more courtroom litigation — including class actions — over plan fees, fiduciary decisions, and denied benefits, and could no longer resolve those disputes in private, individual arbitration. Plan documents would also have to be updated within a year.

drawbacks.text: Employers and plan sponsors argue arbitration resolves disputes faster and more cheaply than court; the bill would shift plan disputes — including class actions — into litigation, raising legal and administrative costs that could be passed on to plans and their participants.

The bill applies immediately to claims arising after enactment, even before plan documents are updated (with a one-year grace period from enforcement penalties), creating a transition period where the rules governing disputes differ from plan paperwork.
Requiring courts to review benefit denials de novo, without deferring to the plan administrator, would mean more merits litigation over individual benefit decisions rather than faster resolution.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers the benefits are concrete: without a ban on class-action waivers, a worker with a small individual loss — say a slice of excessive 401(k) fees — often has no economical way to pursue it, and forced arbitration plus a banned class action closes every door at once. The costs fall mainly on employers and administrators in the form of more litigation, some of which could filter into plan expenses. The bill is a straightforward trade of private, individual arbitration for public, group litigation over workplace benefits.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate's labor committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a vote, or floor action before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Tina Smith introduced the bill on September 25, 2024 — the final months of a two-year Congress — and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
The committee took no further action; the bill sat there with no hearing or vote listed, and Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers, plan sponsors, and benefits administrators that use mandatory arbitration clauses and class-action waivers in retirement and health plans are better off: they keep routing benefit disputes into private arbitration, and workers who lose money through plan fees or denied benefits still have no practical path to a class action. Workers who might have used the law gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and plan administrators kept forced arbitration

for.name: Tina Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on September 25, 2024.

against.name: Bernie Sanders
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Committee never scheduled a hearing or vote on the bill during the roughly three months it was pending before Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the sponsor was a Democrat and no senator of either party signed on as a cosponsor, so no partisan lineup can be measured from the record.

industries.industry: Employers sponsoring retirement and health benefit plans
industries.note: The bill would strip employers of forced arbitration, class-action waivers, and clauses that defer to the plan's own interpretation in benefit disputes, exposing them to more — and pooled — lawsuits from workers and retirees. Its interest in this bill runs against employees' ability to sue over plan losses.

Third-party administrators and insurers operating plans are 'covered persons' prohibited from requiring or agreeing to arbitration and waiver clauses, and they would face de novo court review of benefit denials instead of deferential review.
Pre-dispute arbitration of ERISA plan disputes would become unenforceable, eliminating a stream of workplace benefit cases that would otherwise be heard in private arbitration rather than court.

By invalidating class and collective claim waivers, the bill would open a new docket of group lawsuits over retirement plan fees and denied benefits — the same cases workers would use to recover losses.
